title: Prefix caching technical deep dive - Lumina AI
summary: Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Lumina AI's conversational product. Discussed hit-rate expectations, cache key design (tenant isolation vs sharing), safety/tokenization impacts, eviction/TTL policies, interaction with batching and KV cache size, plus implications for VPC and on-prem deployments. Agreed next steps to run targeted KV-cache benchmarks and share a benchmark spreadsheet and security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-25
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (Lumina CTO), Samira Khan (Lumina Head of ML Infra), Derek Wu (Lumina Senior DevOps)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - i'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood side, and priya is our systems SE. we scheduled this as a deep dive on prefix caching strategies.
[00:18] Priya: hi all, great to be here. can you kick off with your primary goals for caching in your workload, alex?
[00:25] Alex: yeah, sure. our main thing is reducing token costs for long-running conversations, we have a lot of repeated system prompts and user role messages across sessions. target is to cut token generation cost by 30%-50% without adding latency.
[00:38] Samira: and from infra side, we're sensitive about multi-tenant leakages. we run multiple customers in a shared cluster in prod; we want caching but not any risk of cross-tenant inference or cache key collisions.
[00:52] Priya: totally. that's a common ask. a quick overview: Redwood supports prefix/prompt caching at the KV layer - we cache key-value states for common prefixes (like system prompts plus the first few user messages). hit rates depend on how you construct the cache key, TTL/eviction, and prompt variability.
[01:10] Derek: do you hash entire prompt text, or do you do some normalized key? we've seen noise like timestamps or ephemeral ids break keys.
[01:20] Priya: good question. in hosted mode we usually hash a normalized canonicalization of the prefix: strip timestamps, normalize whitespace, replace session-unique placeholders with tokens. that gets us good dedup without leaking. but normalization needs customer buy-in because it changes what counts as a cache hit.
[01:37] Alex: what's the recommended key composition for multi-tenant safety? i.e., do we always include tenant id and model version in the key?
[01:44] Jordan: yes, include tenant id, model id/version, and a normalization hash. including tenant id is non-negotiable for shared clusters; it guarantees namespace isolation even if the hashed text collides. model version ensures deterministic KV semantics across rollouts.
[01:59] Priya: also consider including quantization profile and prompt preprocessor version in the key - those can affect exact token logits.
[02:08] Samira: i'd like to understand hit rate expectations. with our mix (about 40% repetitive system+user prefixes, rest dynamic), what should we expect?
[02:18] Priya: from our benchmarks, if you normalize and group by tenant, typical hit rates are 15%-35% on first-turn prefixes for chat apps; for systems with canned flows it can be 50%+. you sent us a histogram earlier, alex?
[02:29] Alex: yes, attached. our median prompt length is 1.2k tokens, 90th is 3.8k. lots of templates with variable fields.
[02:38] Priya: ok that distribution means KV cache size matters; for 1.2k median you should budget more memory per cached entry. also longer prefixes mean less benefit per token because you save later tokens - but large prefixes increase cache value for subsequent turns.
[02:54] Derek: how do you handle eviction and TTL? we worry about cold starts if we evict too aggressively.
[03:01] Priya: Redwood supports LRU-style eviction with configurable weights by token-length and frequency. recommended for multi-tenant is frequency-biased eviction so hot templates stay. TTLs can be set per-tenant; we usually suggest a sliding TTL (e.g., 24-72 hours) for high reuse workloads.
[03:17] Alex: what's the overhead of checking the KV cache on each request? added latency?
[03:22] Priya: negligible in our runtime - check is O(1) in memory. the real cost is cache miss path where you may incur additional branching for fallback to full decoding. in steady state with hit rates above ~10% we see net tok/latency gains.
[03:36] Jordan: remember batching also affects this - if you batch many short requests, cache hits can amplify throughput. but cache lookups don't coalesce across tenants.
[03:45] Samira: can prefix caching be used with quantized models? we use 4-bit QAT in dedicated clusters.
[03:52] Priya: yes, but you must include quantization profile in the cache key. small quantization differences can change outputs subtly; if you don't namespace keys by quant profile you risk quality regressions. we tested INT4 vs INT8 and saw small but measurable differences in ranking-sensitive tasks.
[04:09] Alex: ok. on private deployments (VPC / on-prem), is the cache local to the node or shared across the cluster? we want to avoid cross-tenant sharing, but also want high hit rates.
[04:21] Priya: options: per-node local KV cache (fast, private) or a shared in-cluster sharded cache with tenant namespace. for strict isolation, per-node local cache with tenant id in key is simplest. for better hit rates across nodes, we offer a sharded cache service that respects tenant namespaces and runs inside the customer's VPC.
[04:40] Derek: if we use the sharded cache in our VPC, do you rely on our Redis/managed cache? any security concerns?
[04:47] Jordan: we can integrate with your managed caches (Redis/KeyDB) in the VPC. we recommend using private subnets + encryption in transit. for on-prem we provide an operator that runs the sharded cache as a statefulset - keys are namespaced by tenant and optionally encrypted at rest using the host KMS.
[05:03] Samira: great. do you store any PII in the cache? our policy disallows persistent storage of user-identifiable text.
[05:11] Priya: by default we store the canonicalized prefix hash and associated KV token states (not the raw prompt text). you can enable a mode where only hashes are stored (no raw text) and set short TTLs. for sensitive workloads we recommend disabling raw-text caching and leaning on per-request private caching.
[05:28] Alex: what's the worst-case degradation if a cache key is stale or mismatched across model rollouts?
[05:34] Priya: stale KV can produce off-by-one or subtle hallucination regressions. that's why model-versioned keys and rolling invalidation are critical. Redwood supports automated cache invalidation on model rollouts and a canary mode where only a percentage of traffic uses cached prefixes until validated.
[05:51] Derek: about benchmarks - can we run a sim that replays our session traces to measure hit rates and latency savings?
[05:57] Priya: yes. recommended: replay with normalization rules you plan to use, vary TTL/eviction policies, and test with quantized and non-quantized models. we'll provide a harness that plugs into your trace exporter.
[06:08] Jordan: we'll share the spreadsheet with expected metrics: per-prefix frequency, baseline tokens generated, cached-token savings, estimated $ savings.
[06:15] Samira: any gotchas with tokenization differences across models? some retokenize slightly differently on open-source variants.
[06:22] Priya: include tokenizer version in key metadata. also, when you switch models mid-session we recommend strict compatibility checks; if tokenization differs we fallback to cold decode for safety.
[06:33] Alex: latency target we care about is 120ms p95 for interactive flows. do you think caching helps there?
[06:40] Priya: yes, for p95 caching tends to shave off the incremental decoding time for repeated prefixes; combined with batching and KV prefetching you can meet 120ms p95 more consistently. but for very long prompts the initial decode will still dominate.
[06:53] Derek: what's the storage footprint you'd expect for our workload (avg 1.2k tokens, 100k active tenants)?
[07:01] Priya: rough guesstimate: if you store compressed KV states per prefix and average 2 prefixes per tenant cached, multiply by kv-state size (which depends on model heads/k/v sizes) - we'd work up exact numbers in the benchmark. likely several tens to low hundreds of GB for active hotset.
[07:18] Alex: that helps. any recommendations for mix of per-node vs sharded cache for us?
[07:23] Priya: start with per-node local cache + tenant namespacing to get isolation and low ops. if hit rates are low and you see cross-node duplication, move to sharded cache inside VPC. we can help size and provision.
[07:36] Jordan: quick recap: include tenant ID, model version, tokenizer version, quant profile, and preproc version in cache key; normalize templates to improve hits; use frequency-biased eviction; enable model-rollout invalidation; and run trace replay benchmarks.
[07:52] Samira: perfect. next steps then?
[07:55] Jordan: priya will share the harness and spreadsheet; we'll schedule the replay benchmark; lumina will deliver anonymized trace histograms. we'll also share security docs and diagrams.
[08:06] Alex: thanks, this was super useful.
[08:09] Derek: thanks everyone.
[08:11] Priya: thanks - we'll follow up with concrete configs and a short runbook for cache settings.

Notes & links: benchmark harness (internal link), security docs (Redwood Private VPC deck), replay spreadsheet (shared drive link)

End of transcript
